options: The plan is general and long-lived; the strategy is project-specific
The strategy is the general approach; the plan applies it to a specific project, release or level
questions.explanation: The strategy is general and lasts across projects. The plan is specific and has a shorter lifespan.

questions.prompt: A test plan should be updated when scope, risk or dates change.
questions.explanation: Plans are living documents; an outdated plan misleads the team.

questions.prompt: Which ISO/IEC/IEEE standard provides a reference structure for test documentation, including the test plan?
questions.explanation: 29119-3 covers test documentation. ISO 9001 is quality management, 27001 is information security and IEEE 754 is floating point.

questions.prompt: Which items typically belong in a test plan? Select all that apply.
options: The source code of the product
questions.explanation: Plans record agreements on scope, resources, schedule and criteria. Source code is not part of a plan.

questions.prompt: A project test plan repeats 15 pages of the organisation's test strategy. Why is that a problem?
options: Duplication causes the copies to diverge and makes the plan hard to read; reference the strategy instead
questions.explanation: Referencing keeps one source of truth and lets the plan focus on project-specific decisions.

questions.prompt: How can an agile team avoid test planning becoming bureaucracy?
options: Keep a short, living plan or test approach covering scope, risk, environments and criteria, tailored to the team
questions.explanation: Agile teams still plan; they keep it light and updated. No planning loses shared agreement.

questions.prompt: The test plan says 'testing will be completed when time runs out'. What is wrong?
options: There are no objective exit criteria, so nobody can say what 'done' means or what risk remains
It should list every test case
questions.explanation: Exit criteria make completion measurable. Time alone says nothing about coverage or quality.

questions.prompt: Halfway through a release, the business adds a new payment provider. The plan was approved a month ago. What should the test lead do?
options: Ignore it, the plan is approved
Assess the new risk, update the plan (scope, effort, schedule, environments), and agree the changes with stakeholders
questions.explanation: Change in scope and risk must be reflected in the plan and agreed. Ignoring or silently absorbing it hides the risk.

questions.prompt: A company has no test strategy; each project does something different and outcomes vary a lot. What is the best first step?
options: Draft a short strategy of shared principles (levels, risk approach, tools, environments, reporting) with the teams and let plans reference it
questions.explanation: A strategy needs agreement from those who use it. Short, shared and referenced is more successful than a large imposed document.
